What she noticed, and did not say aloud, was that she argued better for the student than she had ever argued for the school, and she still could not tell whether that was because the position was truer or merely because it was easier to feel.

Ms. Henry came through the Rotunda at noon with a clipboard, checking the rooms assigned for the mock panel. She stopped when she saw the three of them still going, Rosalie refereeing, Sahil on his feet objecting to something Keira had said thirty seconds earlier.

"Ms. Vasquez," Ms. Henry said, reading the name off her list, "you're first after lunch. Room two." Then, as she turned, she added the thing Keira had been dreading and waiting for in equal measure. "The panel will flip you at some point. They always do. You'll argue the side you believe and then the one you don't, and they'll be watching to see if you can tell the difference."

Keira looked down at her two stacks of cards, the black ink and the blue, sitting side by side on the bench. She squared them together, slid them into the folder, and stood up.

"Room two," she said. "I'm ready."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Caramelization is the browning of sugar on its own, without proteins; table sugar begins to caramelize at about 170 degrees Celsius.
story:
Arianna set the portable burner on the picnic table because the kitchen was being repainted and her mother had banned all cooking indoors until Saturday. The dinner itself was under control, chicken already resting under foil on a warm tray, but the dessert had to happen here, outside, in the wind: a caramel sauce to pour over sliced oranges, which was the only dessert anyone in her family agreed on. Her father's side of the family was coming at seven, and her father had already asked twice whether she was sure she didn't want to just buy ice cream.

The sugar was in the pan, plain white table sugar with a splash of water, and Arianna was watching it the way she had watched it in chemistry class last spring. That was where she had written it down in her notes, and she had transcribed the line into her recipe card that afternoon so she wouldn't forget it at the grill table: caramelization is the browning of sugar on its own, without proteins, and table sugar begins to caramelize at about 170 degrees Celsius. She had no thermometer with her. The wind had knocked the clip-on one off the table an hour ago and cracked it, so she was back to the older method, judging by color and smell, which was exactly the kind of guessing she had spent all year learning not to trust.

"You're staring at it," said Kevin, who had come over through the back gate with a bag of oranges because he'd been assigned fruit duty. "It's sugar. It just sits there until it doesn't."

"That's the problem. It sits there, then it goes fast." She stirred once and put the spoon down. In class, Mr. Santos had drilled them on precision, on waiting for a number, on never trusting an eyeball when an instrument existed. Her grandmother, on the other hand, had made caramel her whole life by color alone, amber and no further, and had never once cracked a thermometer. Two ways of thinking about the same pan, and Arianna had spent the last twenty minutes trying to decide which one she actually believed in, if either, alone at a picnic table with neither a working thermometer nor a grandmother.

Kevin peered into the pan. "It's still clear."

"Then we wait." The wind moved the branches above them and a sullen grey cloud had been sitting on the horizon since five, not raining, not leaving. She thought about her math homework, still unfinished inside, about the graph of the sugar's temperature climbing toward the point where the change began, how the reading rose and rose and the transformation waited, and how a curve that approaches a line without ever touching it, an asymptote, was a useful picture for anything that crept up on you. Except this wasn't that. The sugar would cross its line. It was only a question of when she would notice.

The edges went pale gold first. She turned the burner down a notch and lifted the pan, swirling it, and the whole surface shifted to the color of weak tea and then, faster than she had prepared for, toward amber. Mr. Santos would have said pull it at the number, 170, but the number was gone with the cracked thermometer, and her grandmother's voice in her memory said amber, girl, and she realized she had already made her decision before the thinking finished: she was pulling it at amber, and she was pulling it early, because the pan kept cooking after it left the flame and burnt caramel could not be fixed.

She took it off. A minute later the color deepened on its own into a proper copper and stopped. She added the cream in a careful stream, jumping back when it hissed, and stirred until it went smooth and glossy, and Kevin said, "Okay, that actually smells amazing," which was the most direct compliment he had paid anything since the finals.

She tasted it from the spoon. It was good, and she knew it was also partly luck, and she decided she could hold both of those facts at once. Next time she would have a thermometer, and she would still watch the color, because one had bailed her out tonight and the other had been the reason she knew what to watch for. She poured the sauce into a bowl, set it beside the sliced oranges, and heard her father's car in the front drive.

"Tell them it took twenty minutes," Kevin said.

"Tell them the truth. Tell them it took a whole year of chemistry and one cracked thermometer." She carried the bowl toward the kitchen door, then stopped and called back over her shoulder, "And Kevin, bring the oranges."

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: On a closed interval, a function's largest value can occur at an endpoint where the derivative is not zero, so the endpoints must be checked as well.
story:
The tutoring centre smelled of dry-erase marker and the oranges Mr. Sutton kept in a bowl by the door, ostensibly for students but mostly for himself, since he ate two per session and blamed the missing count on an obstreperous group of seventh graders he refused to name. Sienna slid into her usual seat by the window, the one with a view of the parking lot and, if she leaned far enough, the frozen yogurt place where Sage had started working and where, as of Tuesday, Sage's ex also worked, a fact Sage mentioned four times on the walk over.

"Derivatives," Mr. Sutton said, capping his orange-flavored pen. "Again. Because someone, and I will not malign her, though she is sitting right there, wrote 'the maximum is where the derivative equals zero' on her quiz and then moved on with her life."

"That's what you told us," Sienna said.

"I told you that about the curve. You gave me an interval, with ends, like a fence around the function, and you never once checked the fence."

Rex, across the table, made a low noise of solidarity. Rex had a highlighter in three colours and a system nobody understood, and he had lost six marks on the same quiz for finding a critical point, declaring victory, and never looking left or right again.

"You too?" Sienna said.

"Six marks," Rex said. "I drew a beautiful arrow. It went downhill both ways from my point. I was so proud."

She thought of the quiz then, the way she'd felt that afternoon: the question about a farmer enclosing a pen, or a machine running between two settings, something bounded, and she'd set the derivative to zero, solved, boxed the answer in her neatest handwriting, and felt that clean click of a lock closing. Mr. Sutton had written one word in red at the margin, "ends?", and she had stared at it for a full minute before handing the quiz back, because she genuinely had not known what he was asking.

"Okay," she said now, pulling the quiz out of her binder, flattened from being sat on. "Show me where I went wrong. Not tell me. I want to find it."

Mr. Sutton's whole face did the thing it did when a student said the magic words. He drew a closed interval on the board, a smooth hill of a function inside it, and sat down at his desk and peeled an orange and said nothing further, which was his version of generosity.

She computed. The critical point sat comfortably inside the interval, derivative zero, slope flat, textbook-perfect, and its value came out to something respectable. She was already reaching for the highlighter when Rex leaned over.

"You're about to do the thing," he said.

"I'm not doing the thing."

"You're boxing it. That's the thing."

She looked at the interval again, at the two little filled-in endpoints, the fence Mr. Sutton had drawn, and thought, fine, and evaluated the function at the right-hand end, mostly to prove the end was boring. The right-hand end was not boring. The right-hand end was larger than her critical point, larger by enough that there was no arguing with it, a value sitting out at the edge with a nonzero slope, marching upward right off the page.

"Wait," she said. "Wait, wait."

"There it is," Rex said, solemn as a preacher.

"The biggest value is at the end? The derivative isn't even zero there. It's still climbing."

Mr. Sutton, from behind his orange, said only, "Mm."

"So the whole find-where-it-flattens thing only tells you about the middle. The ends are a whole other stratum you have to dig through separately." She wrote both endpoint values into the margin, lined them up against the critical value like suspects in a lineup, and circled the winner, which was not the elegant interior point she'd been so proud of ten minutes earlier. "Rex. Your six marks. You have to test the endpoints too, both of them, every time. Not just the pretty critical point."

Rex looked personally betrayed by mathematics. "I highlighted the critical point in yellow," he said. "I highlighted it like it mattered."

"It mattered. It just didn't win."

They worked through three more problems together, Rex reading numbers aloud like a bingo caller, Sienna at the board calling out the endpoint values and the critical value and comparing, always comparing, because skipping the comparison was how the marks died. Somewhere in the middle of the second one Sage texted a photo from the yogurt shop: her ex at the register, captioned "hostile stratum of my life." Sienna typed back "test the endpoints" and got back three question marks and a ghost emoji.

She couldn't fully explain it yet, honestly. Why the rule only held inside the fence and dissolved at the border was something she could demonstrate but not yet narrate, and she wrote that in the margin of her notes, in small letters, "ask later," because pretending she understood more than she did was exactly the error that had cost her the quiz.

At nine, Mr. Sutton collected the markers and said, "Same time Thursday. Bring your fence posts."

Rex held the door. Outside, the yogurt shop glowed across the lot, and Sage's shape was visible at the counter next to the shape she kept texting about.

"Endpoint run before the parking lot?" Rex said, jingling his keys. "For closure."

"For closure," Sienna said, and they cut across the dark grass toward the light.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: US food safety agencies say chicken is safely cooked when its internal temperature reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer.
story:
Nevaeh stood at the grill in the backyard with a pair of tongs in one hand and a plate of raw chicken in the other, and she felt like a surgeon about to operate without a licence. Her parents were at the hospital visiting her grandmother, her brother was at soccer, and dinner was, for once, entirely her problem. She had volunteered for it in a moment of ambition she now regarded the way one regards an old haircut, with affection and regret.

"You're staring at it," said Peyton from the picnic table, where she was supposedly collating the recipes Nevaeh had printed out and had instead arranged into a fan. "It's chicken. It can't stare back."

"It can betray me," Nevaeh said. "That's worse."

Peyton had come over under the pretence of helping, which so far had meant eating the cheese reserved for the salad and offering commentary. Lorelei was supposed to arrive by six with dessert, which gave Nevaeh ninety minutes to produce a meal worthy of the text she had sent her mother, the one that said, with breathtaking confidence, Don't worry about dinner, I have it handled.

The chicken went onto the grate with a hiss that sounded official. She turned it once, twice, then made her first mistake: she flipped it again, having read somewhere that confident grillers flip often, and having confused confidence with knowledge. By the time the outside looked right, she had no idea about the inside, and she had a vivid memory to blame for her nerves.

Two summers ago at her uncle's place, she had eaten a chicken breast that looked cooked, all golden and innocent, and had spent the following night becoming personally acquainted with the concept of immunology, or at least with her mother lecturing her about immune systems while holding her hair back. Ever since, she had treated poultry as a suspect that could not be trusted on appearance alone, though she couldn't have said what to trust instead. Her mother cut into the middle and looked. Her grandmother pressed it with a fork. Both methods felt like reading tea leaves.

Now she cut into the thickest breast, and the juices ran clear-ish, possibly, in the fading light. She squinted. Peyton squinted with her, in solidarity.

"Is that pink or is that just the sunset?" Peyton asked.

"That's the kind of question that ruins lives," Nevaeh said.

She was still deliberating when the back gate rattled and her father came through it, hospital visiting hours having ended early because her grandmother had thrown out her hip trying to escape the physiotherapist. He took in the scene: his daughter, the tongs, the half-opened breast, the expression of a person defusing a bomb.

"Hold on," he said, and set down his jacket and went into the kitchen, and came back holding a thin metal wand with a dial at the top, which he handed over like a sceptre. "Instant-read thermometer. Been in the drawer since forever."

Nevaeh turned it over. "Why do you have this and never use it?"

"Why do you have a bread maker and never use it? We're a family of unused appliances." He tapped the probe. "US food safety agencies say chicken is safely cooked when its internal temperature reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit. That's about 74 degrees Celsius, if you think in metric."

"I don't, but thank you." She stabbed the probe into the thickest part of the breast, angling it sideways the way it seemed to want, and watched the needle climb. It passed 120, paused as though considering, kept going. The breasts that looked perfect, the ones she would have proudly served, read 158 and 161, which sounded close and also sounded, in her current state of paranoia, like roulette.

The one that had looked slightly pale, the one she'd been ashamed of, read 167.

"Peyton," she said slowly, "the ugly one is the safe one."

"The ugly one is always the safe one," Peyton said. "Have you met my dating history?"

Nevaeh laughed so hard she nearly dropped the thermometer into the coals. Then she put the pale-looking breast back on the grill, waited, and watched the needle settle past 165, and only then moved it to the platter. The golden ones she cooked longer too, out of a stubbornness she admitted to nobody, because they were the ones her eyes had vouched for and her eyes, it turned out, were charlatans.

Lorelei arrived at six with a lemon tart and the announcement that she was destitute, having spent her entire paycheque on the tart's ingredients, and therefore would be accepting dinner as payment in kind. They ate at the picnic table under the string lights, her father home early, her brother texting that he'd eaten at practice, her grandmother reportedly demanding pudding from a full-body cast. The chicken was juicy in a way that surprised everyone, including the chicken.

"I always thought the thermometer people were obsessive," Nevaeh said, licking a thumb. "Like the kind of people who weigh their flour."

"Twenty minutes ago you were going to serve us all a gamble," her father said.

"Twenty minutes ago I was a different chef." She held up the probe, twirling it. "This thing's mine now. It lives with my knives."

Down at the end of the table, Peyton was already reaching for the last breast, the pale-looking one, the best one of the lot. "Mine," she said.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In Kahlo's Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird (1940), the dead hummingbird hanging at her throat is a Mexican folk charm for luck in love.
story:
Jasmine spread the print of Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird across the picnic table and weighted its corners with stones from her mother's flowerbed, because the backyard wind in August treated paper like a personal insult. Kenley sat across from her with her laptop open, and Kiptyn lay on the grass with his copy of the assignment sheet held above his face, reading it for the fourth time as though the words might rearrange themselves into something easier.

"Formal analysis," Kenley said. "Colour, composition, symbolism. That's the whole rubric. Two pages. Mr. Moose wants us to look, not feel."

"That's the problem," Jasmine said. "I look and all I do is feel." She bent close to the print. Kahlo's face fronted the viewer, level and unblinking, framed by leaves and a cat and a monkey, the thorn necklace cutting a dark line into her neck. Behind her, the green was so dense it flattened into a wall. She had spent an hour last night trying to decide whether the background pressed forward or receded, and had written nothing.

Kiptyn rolled onto his elbow. "It's a bird," he said, tapping the small black shape dangling at her throat. "It's dead. That's basically all I've got. Maybe it's just decoration. Frida liked weird stuff."

Jasmine was quiet for a moment. The bird bothered her the way a wrong note bothers someone who can't name intervals. It hung at the exact center of the painting, below the mouth, above the folded hands, and paintings did not put decoration at the center. "It's not decoration," she said, but she could not yet say what it was, and the not-knowing sat in her chest like a stone.

Her grandmother came out with a tray of limonada, moving slowly across the grass in her housecoat, and stopped behind Jasmine's shoulder. She set down the tray, then leaned in, squinting at the dead bird. Something shifted in her face. "Ay, el colibrí," she said. Then, in English, for the benefit of the table: "That is a Mexican folk charm. For luck in love."

Kiptyn sat up so fast his assignment sheet fluttered loose. "Wait. The dead bird is a love charm?"

"Dead things can still be charms," Jasmine's grandmother said, and poured the lemonade, and went back inside, leaving them with that.

Jasmine felt something open, not like an answer but like a door onto a longer hallway. She pulled her notebook over and began to write fast, her pen skating. The charm for luck in love, hung at the throat, directly beneath the mouth that cannot ask; the thorns cutting the same neck the charm is meant to bless; the animals arranged in a symmetry that was almost sedimentary, layered leaf on leaf on creature, so that the portrait seemed fossilized inside its own longing. She was not sure yet whether the hummingbird mocked the wish or protected it, and she wrote that down too, the uncertainty, because it was the truest thing she had. Luck in love, from a bird that was already dead. The painting held both ideas at once, and refusing to choose between them might itself be the analysis.

"Read it to me," Kenley said. "The symbolism part."

Jasmine read aloud. When she finished, the yard was very quiet except for a real hummingbird, an impossible green blur, working the trumpet vine by the fence. It hovered, drank, and shot away over the shed, alive in every way the painted one was not, and all three of them watched it go.

"That," Kiptyn said softly. "Put that in the paper. Not the bird, the watching."

She didn't think a rubric could grade a moment of watching, but she wrote it down anyway, one line at the bottom of the page: the charm is dead, and the vine is full of living birds. She underlined it twice, closed the notebook, and helped Kenley gather the stones from the corners before the wind could take anything else.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Paul Boyer and John Walker shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for explaining how ATP synthase makes ATP.
story:
The exam was in nine days, and Noemie had chosen to study cellular respiration in a community garden, which even she could admit was a bit much. She sat on an upturned crate between the raspberry canes and the compost bins with her textbook open on her knees, and every time she read the word "mitochondrion" a wasp read it over her shoulder.

"Still on glycolysis?" Eli arrived with a paper bag of plums and sat down on the grass without asking, which was how things worked between them. He was the one person in their biology class who actually understood the whole pathway, and he knew it, and he was mostly gracious about it, except when he wasn't.

"I'm past glycolysis. I'm at the part where everything goes into the mitochondria and gets taken apart by the cycle with the terrible name."

"The Krebs cycle."

"That's the one." She tapped the diagram, a circle of arrows that looked like a municipal recycling logo. "I can memorize it but I can't hold it. It slides off by morning."

Eli chewed a plum and considered the problem the way he considered most things, sideways. "You know what Mr. Girma does down here on Saturdays? He keeps a little library in the shed. Old textbooks, seed catalogs, someone's abandoned nursing school notes. You could look at it from another angle."

She found Mr. Girma tying up tomato stakes, a tall man in a shirt printed with birds who had signed off on her volunteer hours for two years without ever learning her name. The shed was cool and smelled of string and cut grass. The library was three shelves of surrendered ambition, and among the nursing notes and a water-stained copy of a Norwegian seed catalog, its photographs of fjord-side allotments gone soft and purple, she found a thin paperback on the history of biochemistry with a cracked spine.

She took it back to the crate. Eli had fallen asleep against the compost bins with the plum bag deflating on his chest, which she took as permission to ignore him.

The book had a chapter on ATP, the cell's currency, and she read that for years nobody knew how the last step actually worked, how the enzyme built the stuff. Then a page she nearly skipped. Two men had worked it out, Paul Boyer and John Walker, and for that they had shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. She read the sentence twice. She had been lying awake trying to force the pathway into her head as one more thing to memorize, and here it turned out that a piece of it, the enzyme at the very end, had been a mystery serious enough to win a Nobel.

"Wake up," she said, and threw a raspberry leaf at Eli.

He woke complaining. She showed him the page.

"So it's hard," he said, when he'd finished. "It's hard for Nobel laureates."

"It's not hard in the way I thought. I've been treating it like a map, like if I trace the arrows enough times I'll know the city. But it's a machine. Somebody had to figure out what the machine does, and it took them decades, and I'm annoyed at myself for needing two weeks."

Eli peeled another plum. "That's a very cosmopolitan crisis you're having. Some people fail the exam and move on with their lives."

"Some people weren't promised to a biology program in September."

They walked the rows while she recited what she had, and he corrected her the way you'd steady a cup someone was carrying, lightly, from the side. Glucose split in the cytoplasm. The pieces moved inward, into the mitochondria, through the cycle with the terrible name, and the point of all of it, she said, slowing down, was not the carbon going out the chimney but the small charged streams that turned the final wheel. She was still saying it wrong in places. He told her which places.

Near the gate, Ibrahim from her chemistry class was filling jugs at the tap, and he asked what she was doing there with a textbook on a Saturday. She told him about the enzyme, and the prize, and then found she couldn't stop: she said that what she liked was that the diagram in the textbook had a date on its conscience, that somebody in a lab had gone from not knowing to knowing, and that the arrows on her page were the residue of an argument, not a fact that had always been lying around.

"That's either very deep or you're stalling," Ibrahim said.

"Both, probably. I still can't recite it clean. Ask me Tuesday."

She sat back down on the crate as the afternoon shifted. She would try again tonight, tracing glucose down through the stages to the wheel that made the ATP, and some of it would slide off by morning, and she would bring it back the next day, and she could not yet say whether she was learning the material or learning how to be someone who learned material, though she suspected, uncomfortably, that it was the second, and that it would take longer than nine days. The wasp had gone. Eli handed her the last plum without opening his eyes, and she took it.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: The last time a British monarch refused royal assent to a bill was in 1708, when Queen Anne vetoed the Scottish Militia Bill.
story:
Joseph had been blase about the whole thing until Tuesday, when he found out the bill would actually die in committee. He had written it himself, all four pages, after the pools at Harrowfield Park stopped opening on weekends in September. His bill proposed that city recreation facilities stay open through October, with evening hours funded by a small increase in the parking levy downtown. Mr. Owusu, who taught civics and had somehow persuaded the city council to let the youth parliament use its chamber for one Saturday session, had read the draft and said only, "Resubmit it with a fiscal note attached." Joseph had resubmitted it three times.

The chamber smelled like floor polish and old paper. Joseph sat in the second row of the curved desks, his name placard in front of him, watching the public gallery fill. His mother was up there, unwrabling a cough drop too loudly. Fatoumata slid into the seat beside him with a binder the size of a paving stone. "You're on second reading," she said. "After the zoning thing. Don't let them talk you out of the fiscal note, because they will try."

The morning went to other business first. A councilwoman moved an amendment to the transit bylaw, and Joseph watched something he had not expected: a bill was not a fixed thing but a living document, bent and reworked clause by clause. Members rose, objected, withdrew, reintroduced. When they finally voted, hands undulated across both sides of the chamber like grass in wind, and the clerk counted aloud, and the amendment passed by two votes, and the whole bill went back to committee, again, after six weeks of work. Joseph wrote in his notes: this is slow on purpose. He was not sure yet whether that was a defense or an indictment.

Then the Speaker called his bill. Joseph stood, arranged his pages, and read the opening statement he had rehearsed against the bathroom mirror. He talked about Harrowfield, about the October evenings when the light lasted until seven and every gate in the city was chained at five. He had numbers. He had a petition with three hundred and eleven signatures, gathered by Fatoumata outside the library and by Paige at the skate park, and he tabled it with hands that were steadier than he had any right to expect.

A member from the north district rose to oppose. "The levy is regressive," she said, "and your clause four conflicts with the existing facility bylaw." Joseph had an answer for the levy, which Fatoumata had helped him build, about phased exemptions for low-income permit holders. He had no answer for clause four, because he had not known clause four conflicted with anything. He said so, out loud, into the microphone, and the chamber made a small sound, half sympathy, half amusement, and he felt his ears go hot. But Fatoumata was already flipping through her binder, and she stood on a point of information and read out the subsection his clause contradicted, and moved that the bill be referred back to committee for reconciliation rather than defeated outright. The vote carried.

They broke for lunch on the steps of city hall. Paige sat down beside him with two sandwiches and gave him one. "You looked like you were going to pass out when she caught clause four," she said.

"I almost did," Joseph said. "Fatoumata saved it."

"That's what a committee is for, technically." Paige peeled the crust off her sandwich in one long strip. "Anyway, the real drama is this afternoon. I have to give royal assent, and I'm thinking about refusing."

Joseph stopped chewing. Paige, as the oldest member of the youth parliament in good standing, had been assigned the lieutenant governor's role for the session, the stand-in for the Crown, with the ceremonial duty of signing bills into law after they passed. "You can't refuse," he said.

"Why not? It's my signature."

He genuinely did not know, and it bothered him more than clause four had. He took out his phone and searched while Paige ate, and there it was, in a parliamentary reference site, plain as anything: the last time a British monarch refused royal assent to a bill was in 1708, when Queen Anne vetoed the Scottish Militia Bill. Three hundred years and more, and it had never happened again. He read it twice. "The last time a British monarch refused royal assent to a bill was in 1708," he said. "Queen Anne vetoed the Scottish Militia Bill. Nobody has done it since."

"So it's legal but nobody does it."

"It's more than that," Joseph said slowly, working it out as he spoke. "If you refused, you would be exercising a power that has been asleep for three centuries. Everyone in that chamber would know it. The whole point of you is that you're not supposed to be the point."

Paige looked at him for a moment. "You're arguing against your own bill," she said. "If I refused, your pools stay closed."

"I know." He did know, and it was strange to feel the pull of both. He wanted his bill to live, and he wanted the chamber to keep working the way it had all morning, slow and clumsy and correct. "But you'd be breaking something to get a swimming pool."

The afternoon session droned through the zoning item, and then his bill came back from the reconciliation committee with a rewritten clause four, and the debate was shorter this time, almost gentle, members nodding at the amendments they themselves had forced. The vote was called, and Joseph watched the hands rise around the curve, counting along with the clerk, and it passed, twenty-two to nine. Then the Speaker turned to Paige, seated above them in the chair with a fountain pen she had brought from home, and asked whether His Excellency's deputy was pleased to assent. Paige held the pen above the signature line and let the pause stretch, one second, two, and Joseph's heart climbed into his throat. Then she signed, and the chamber applauded, and Fatoumata leaned over and whispered, "You owe me a sandwich."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: The Maillard reaction, between amino acids and sugars, browns food and creates much of its flavor; it proceeds rapidly at about 140 to 165 degrees Celsius.
story:
Mathis set the chicken thighs skin-down in the pan and listened to the sound they made, which was almost nothing. A thin sigh of steam, a pallid shimmer where moisture gathered at the edges. He had wanted this dinner to work. His mother came home from the late shift at eight, his grandfather ate early and complained regardless, and tonight Mathis had promised both of them something better than the tray of pale, steamed thighs he'd served on Tuesday, which his grandfather had pushed around the plate before saying only, "Chicken shouldn't look like that," and nothing else.

He turned the burner up one notch and waited. The pan was hot before the oil, he had made sure of that, or he had thought he had. The thighs sat there, releasing water, poaching in their own liquid. His grandfather was at the table behind him doing the crossword in pencil, first the across clues, then the down, as though the puzzle owed him an apology.

"Did you let the pan heat all the way?" his grandfather asked, not looking up.

"Until the oil shimmered."

"Hm."

Mathis took out his phone and messaged Lynden, who was doing a food science elective and had once corrected Mr. Sutton in chemistry without flinching. Why does chicken brown in a pan. Lynden answered fast, the way he answered everything, as if delay were a form of losing. It's called the Maillard reaction. Between amino acids and sugars. It's what browns the food and creates most of the flavor. It goes fast around 140 to 165 degrees Celsius. Your pan's too cold, probably.

Mathis looked at the dial, then at the water pooling around the chicken, and understood that he had been patient with the wrong thing. He had internalized the idea that cooking rewarded gentleness, that care meant low heat and slow waiting, and now that idea sat in front of him looking specious, a pleasant theory undone by a thermometer and a phone screen. He lifted the thighs out, poured off the liquid, and set the empty pan back over the highest flame. He was aware of his grandfather watching him now, pencil down.

"Lynden says it needs to be hotter," Mathis said.

"Lynden," his grandfather said, as if tasting the name.

"He's the one who won the regional thing. Mr. Sutton gave him that honorarium for the tutoring he did over the summer, fifty dollars in an envelope, like it was 1975." Mathis wiped the thighs dry with a paper towel, one at a time, the way he had seen his mother do with fish. When a drop of water danced and skittered across the pan's surface and vanished, he laid the chicken back down, and this time the sound was a hiss that filled the kitchen, and the smell changed within a minute into something that made his stomach tighten.

From the doorway, his mother watched him without announcing herself. Her feet ached and she had planned to stand in the shower for ten full minutes before eating anything, but the smell from the kitchen had reached the front hall, dark and savory, and she found she could not pass it. She saw her son bent over the stove, turning the thighs with tongs, the skin gone the color of chestnuts. She saw her father at the table with the crossword folded and forgotten, and she understood, in the wordless way she understood most things about that man, that some approval had already been given, and that it would never be spoken, and that her son did not yet know he had it.

She could also see what Mathis could not: that he was running a small experiment in front of them, testing whether this thing he'd made could stand in for an apology, or a truce, or whatever it was he meant by cooking for the family on a Thursday. She didn't know which. She wasn't sure he did either.

"Dinner's in ten minutes," Mathis said without turning around, because he had seen her reflection in the darkened window over the sink and had decided not to say anything about it, to let her arrival be ordinary.

"Plates are where they always are," his grandfather said.

She got three plates down and set the table while the chicken finished, and when Mathis turned around with the pan, his face was damp at the hairline and lit orange by the stove behind him.

"Careful," he said. "It's hot."

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: Peak bone mass is typically reached in the early twenties in women and the late twenties in men, so bone built in the teenage years affects bone strength for life.
story:
Blake had promised himself he would ask three real questions at the open house, and so far he had asked none, because the campus was bigger than his whole town and every booth seemed to require a confidence he did not have. He had come for the kinesiology program, mostly to prove to his father that it was not, as his father put it, "a degree in jumping jacks." What Blake had not planned on was the phone call two nights before, from his mother, saying his grandmother had slipped on her kitchen mat and broken her hip, and that she was lying in a hospital bed being morose about it, refusing the pudding.

"She said, tell Blake I should have moved more when I was young," his mother had reported, tired in the voice that meant the hospital vending machine had run out of everything but grape soda. "She said that, and then she wouldn't say anything else."

Blake had turned this over for two days. His grandmother was seventy-eight; the slip was the slip of an old woman on a mat, not of a teenager on a soccer field, and it seemed strange to him that she reached for her sixteen-year-old grandson's habits as the place to lay the blame. It was like blaming a barn door for a storm. Still, he had looked up from his phone that night and noticed how many hours he spent folded into a chair, and the thought had followed him onto the bus this morning, all the way to the university's gleaming recreation complex, where the kinesiology booth stood between nutrition and an engineering display involving a small robot that kept falling over.

Harman had come along for the free tote bag, and had already collected four. "You're doing the face," Harman said, appearing at Blake's elbow. "The face you do when you're thinking about something sad and pretending it's about protein."

"It's about my grandma. Broken hip. She's fine, mostly, but she's mad at her younger self." Blake picked up a pamphlet just to have something in his hands. "Can you even fix that later? Like, at seventy?"

"How would I know. Ask the bone people."

"The bone people."

"Those two." Harman pointed with a tote bag at a pair of graduate students behind the booth, one of whom was holding a plastic model of a femur like a microphone and pretending to interview the other. Blake watched this, decided it was the most promising sign of approachable academia he had seen all day, and walked over.

The one with the femur turned out to be studying bone development, and when Blake asked his question, she did not give him a speech. She turned the model over instead and said, "Here's the thing most people don't know. Peak bone mass comes in the early twenties for women and the late twenties for men. After that you're basically living off what you banked." The other student nodded along, chewing a granola bar. "So your grandma's right to be mad, honestly. Bone built in the teenage years is what you carry for life. It's like a retirement account, except you can't get an extension."

Blake stood there a second. He had assumed the body was more forgiving than that, that everything was repairable, that decisions had a statute of limitations. The idea that a choice he made at sixteen, or didn't make, would still be settled into his skeleton at fifty felt both unfair and weirdly clarifying, like finding out the whole building had a foundation and that the foundation was now, this year, while he sat in chairs. He was aware of the truism lurking nearby, the old people always say sort of thing, and he had always filed such sayings under things adults repeat because repeating is easier than thinking. But here was an actual number attached to it, an actual decade, and it came out of a plastic femur at a booth.

"Wait," said Harman, who had drifted over and was listening with the expression of someone doing math he resented. "So if I skip every gym class until I'm twenty-nine, and then panic..."

"You can improve things," the student said, "but you can't fully get back what you didn't build. It's not a crisis. It's just math with consequences." She waggled the femur at them both, cheerfully. "Resistance exercise. Jumping, weirdly, helps. Bones respond to impact."

"Jumping," Harman said. "You're telling me the mandated trampoline of my childhood was medicine."

"It could debilitate you too, if you do it badly," she said. "Everything's like that."

Blake laughed, and it loosened something. He asked his three real questions then, about the program, about the lab, about whether first-years got to touch the equipment or just look at it through glass, and the answers were better than the pamphlet. He wrote his email on the interest sheet with the pen chained to the table. On the walk out, past the falling-over robot, which had now been set upright by an embarrassed engineer, he found he was still carrying the femur conversation the way you carry a stone in a shoe, turning it over with every step. He could not know whether his grandmother's hip would have been spared by anything, whether her twenties or her teens had gone wrong or whether it was only the mat, only luck, and he was honest enough with himself to leave that unresolved. What he did know was that his own late twenties now had a shape to them, faint but real, and that the shape was being decided partly today, partly in the chair he would go home to.

"So," he said to Harman, at the bus stop, hoisting two of Harman's tote bags that had been reassigned to him as tribute. "Trampoline this weekend. My mom has one in the garage from when my cousin lived with us."

"You want to bank bone," Harman said, "on a decade-old trampoline, in a garage."

"Medicine," Blake said, and rang the doorbell chime on the bus as it hissed open.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Psychologist Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups develop through four stages: forming, storming, norming and performing.
story:
The gym smelled like rubber and floor wax, and Emile was missing layups. It was the third practice of the season, and already Aria had stopped passing to him when he cut to the basket, which was understandable, since he'd bricked her last four feeds clean off the backboard. Lawrence, who was pugnacious by nature and had once gotten a technical foul in a scrimmage for arguing with his own teammate, kept shouting for the ball even when he wasn't open. Emile was beginning to wonder what he'd signed up for.

He had signed up in September, in the first week of school, mostly because of a memory he kept returning to. Two years ago, in grade nine, his older cousin had dragged him to watch the senior team practice, and Emile had stood in the doorway watching five boys run a fast break so smoothly it looked like one animal moving. He remembered thinking that this was what he wanted, not the scoring but the moving together, the way a body could belong to something larger than itself. He'd been too nervous to try out that year, or the next. This year he'd written his name on the sheet before he could think about it.

By the end of November, the thinking had gotten bad anyway. They'd lost four of six games, and the bus rides home had turned into arguments. Aria lambasted the defence for collapsing on every screen; Lawrence told her she was ball-hogging; a junior named only as "the kid" by everyone sat in the back with his headphones on and his jaw tight. In the change room after a particularly ugly loss, Emile found Lawrence and Aria shouting at each other over whose fault the last possession had been, and he stood there holding his shoes, wanting to say something and not knowing what.

The coach cleared her throat from the doorway. She was a short woman with a whistle she rarely used. "Storming," she said, mostly to herself, and then, "Bus leaves in ten." She walked out before anyone could ask.

Emile asked anyway, later, at home, with his phone on his stomach. He typed the word and found a psychologist named Bruce Tuckman, who had proposed in 1965 that groups develop through four stages: forming, storming, norming and performing. He read it twice. Forming was the polite part, the first practices, everyone on their best behaviour. Storming was the arguing, the friction, the bus rides home. It had a name. It was, apparently, a stage, which meant it was also a passage, which meant there was something on the other side. Norming and performing sat there on his screen like a promise written by a man fifty years dead.

He wasn't sure he believed it, exactly. It seemed too tidy, the way things in textbooks were tidy, as though a group of twelve teenagers could be graphed. But he brought it to practice anyway, sidling up to Aria while she retied her shoes. "The coach said something weird," he told her. "Storming. I looked it up. This guy Tuckman, 1965, said groups go through four stages. Forming, storming, norming, performing." Aria squinted at him. "So we're the storm part?" "I think we're deep in the storm part." She was quiet for a second, then said, "Then what's norming," and he said he didn't know, and she said, "Figure it out, we play Northgate on Friday," and laced her shoes tighter.

He tried to figure it out. He started small, which felt ridiculous but was all he had. When Lawrence demanded the ball, Emile called out the play instead of rolling his eyes, giving the demand a shape other people could follow. When Aria overhandled, he cut harder to give her a target instead of drifting to the corner to sulk. It wasn't magic. They still lost to Northgate by nine. But in the third quarter, for about four possessions, something clicked: Lawrence screened, Aria read it, Emile flashed to the elbow and hit the fifteen-footer, and nobody celebrated any one of them, because it hadn't belonged to any one of them.

After the game, the kid from the back of the bus was waiting by the water fountain. He'd played six garbage minutes and turned the ball over twice, and earlier that week he'd cracked a clipboard in frustration, and the coach had made him do restitution, mopping the whole floor after practice until it shone. "That Tuckman thing," the kid said. "Aria told me. Which stage is it when you're not fighting anymore but you're also not good yet?" Emile opened his mouth and then closed it, because he honestly didn't know. "Between, maybe," he said. The kid nodded slowly, bouncing his ball twice against the linoleum. "So we're between."

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: Economists count the wages a student gives up while studying full-time as part of the cost of college, along with tuition.
story:
Zachary had the closing shift on Saturdays, which meant sweeping under the pastry case and wiping down the espresso machine while the dour manager counted the drawer behind the counter. Six hours at eleven dollars an hour. He kept the arithmetic in his head the way other people kept songs.

The money was for the car. Six months of Saturdays, plus the birthday cash from his grandmother, had brought him to twenty-one hundred dollars, and the hatchback behind Delaney's uncle's repair shop was listed at twenty-four. Delaney had promised to put in a word. Zachary could already feel the keys in his pocket, the particular freedom of not asking anyone for a ride again.

He was on his break, sipping the burnt espresso the staff called "the house special" in the shop's private vernacular, when Gaelle came in with a folder from the university open house. She slid into the seat across from him and opened it to a worksheet. "You have to look at this," she said. "I thought tuition was the whole cost. But the sheet says economists count the wages you give up while studying full-time as part of the cost of college too, along with tuition. Four years of paychecks. It's not just what you spend, it's what you never earn."

Zachary turned the page toward the window light. The worksheet asked each student to instantiate the idea with an example from their own life, and beside it, in Gaelle's handwriting, was a line about her cousin who had gone straight to work at the hospital laundry and now had an apartment and a dog. "So college costs more than I thought," Gaelle said. "Like, twice as much, almost. I'm rethinking the whole thing."

He meant to say something supportive. Instead he said, "What's the job you'd be giving up?" because he realized he was doing the same math in reverse. If he kept the car money and worked Saturdays through senior year, he'd have maybe eight thousand dollars by June, and a car, and the shifts he'd need to keep the gas tank full. If he spent twelve hundred of it on the summer engineering program at the community college, he'd have no car, and every Saturday he spent at the program would be a Saturday he wasn't paid.

"It's not just the money out," he said slowly. "It's the money that never comes in." He thought of the hatchback, its deflated rear tire, the way it had sat in the lot like a promise. He had been counting only what he spent. He had never once counted what he was choosing not to earn.

Mr. Delgado, the retired teacher from the corner condo who came in every evening for a medium drip, set his cup down at the next table and said, without looking up from his crossword, "My nephew did that arithmetic for two years. Then he did it again and came out the other way." He licked his pencil and said nothing further, which was typical of him.

That night Zachary asked the manager whether the Saturday closing shift could go to someone else for eight weeks, starting in July. The manager said Gaelle had been asking for more hours. Zachary texted her from the back room: want my Saturdays this summer? Her reply came before he'd put the phone down: yes. Seriously? He typed that the program was twelve hundred and the car could wait a year, that the hatchback had a rusted quarter panel anyway, that Delaney's uncle would still be selling cars in September.

On Monday he registered online, and the confirmation page charged his card with a small, final sound. He felt lighter and poorer at the same time, the way you feel after giving something away. When Gaelle came in for her first closing shift, she was wearing the apron wrong and asking the manager questions about the grinder, and Zachary, watching from a corner table with his open textbook, raised his cup to her. She raised the steam wand in reply, like a sword.

The following April, Zachary found the program's follow-up flyer in his backpack: graduates who completed the track were eligible for a paid lab internship, sixteen hours a week, at the university. He read it twice, then texted Gaelle a photo of it. Her answer came back in under a minute: "so you gave up the car to get a job that pays you to learn." He looked at the flyer again, then out the window at the bus pulling up to the corner, and typed: "don't tell the hatchback."

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: The AP 2-D Art and Design portfolio's Selected Works section asks for 5 artworks and counts for 40 percent of the score.
story:
Luca stood in front of a painting of a flooded parking lot and tried to make himself care. The gallery was showing work by artists under twenty-five, which Ms. Wright had called germane to their situation, meaning relevant, meaning she wanted them to feel either inspired or doomed. The portfolio was due in nine days. Ten artworks around one theme, plus an artist's statement he hadn't started, and he still didn't have a theme.

"Stop hovering," Skye said, appearing beside him with a paper cup of water from the reception table. "You're hovering. People think you're guarding it."

"I'm thinking."

"You're glaring at it. There's a difference." She tilted her head at the flooded parking lot. "I like the one back there with the hands."

Everybody liked the one with the hands. Wilson had said so on the bus, and Wilson liked almost nothing, so the hands were probably objectively good, if such a thing existed, which Luca was starting to suspect it didn't, which was itself a problem, because if nothing was objectively good then how was he supposed to choose anything.

They drifted toward the back room, where a girl their age was taping a sketchbook open on a pedestal. Her name card said she was a first-year at the art school downtown. The sketchbook pages were all the same staircase, drawn from different angles, in different weather, one in what looked like charcoal and dish soap.

"Excuse me," Luca said, before he could talk himself out of it. "Did you do all of these about one staircase?"

She looked up, wary the way people are when they suspect they're about to be mocked. "It's my grandmother's staircase. She died in March." A pause. "I couldn't stop drawing it, so I made it the assignment."

Luca nodded. He didn't say anything sympathetic, because anything he said would be worse than silence, and Skye, thank God, just said "It's good," and the girl's shoulders came down half an inch.

On the bus home, Luca got out his phone and opened the College Board page he'd bookmarked in September and read properly for the first time. He'd been so fixed on the ten pieces, the sustained investigation, that he'd skimmed past the rest. Now he read it twice. Skye leaned over his arm.

"Wait, say that part again."

"The Selected Works section asks for five artworks," Luca said. "It counts for forty percent of the score."

"Five pieces. Forty percent." Skye sat back. "So half your grade is basically riding on five images."

"Not half. Forty percent." But he saw her point, which was the problem. He had eleven pieces he liked and he'd been assuming the written part, the investigation, was where the real weight sat. If five physical works carried forty percent of the score, then choosing those five was not a detail. It was the decision.

He spent Tuesday and Wednesday photographing everything in the garage where he worked, because the garage was his grandmother's flooded parking lot, his staircase, his one subject, except he'd never admitted it. He hadn't chosen it; it had requisitioned him, pulled him in and assigned him the job. Eleven images: a bicycle wheel in oil, his father's hands black to the wrist, a calendar of shifts, a wall of hanging tools like a choir. Wilson came over Thursday and spread the prints across the workbench like tarot.

"The wheel one, obviously. The hands, obviously. The tools." Wilson tapped three. "Then what, you've got eight left for two spots."

"That's the part I keep getting wrong," Luca said. "I keep wanting to include the ones that were hard, because they cost the most. Like difficulty is a quality."

"Difficulty is not a quality," Wilson said. "My chemistry grade is proof."

Luca laughed, which he needed, and then went quiet, because the hard ones and the good ones were two different ways of thinking about the same work and he couldn't just pick one. Effort was real; it had made him better; but the portfolio wasn't a record of his suffering, it was an argument about what a garage is at night when only one bulb works. He pulled out two more prints, the ones where the garage was most itself, and set them apart from the ones where he was most himself, and found, relieved, that the two piles overlapped in three places.

Friday, Ms. Wright kept him after class. "Your statement," she said. "Do you have one yet?"

"A sentence. It's not good."

"Say it anyway."

"I'm trying to show that the garage is the last room in the house where things are still fixable."

Ms. Wright was quiet long enough that he checked her face for the polite blank that meant disappointment. It wasn't there. "Write that on a card," she said, "and tape it above your desk, and when you pick your five, ask each one if it agrees with the card."

He worked all weekend. Sunday night his father came into the garage with two sandwiches and stood over the five finalists lined on the hood of the dead Toyota, and Luca, mouth full, explained the forty percent, the five works, the whole structure of the thing, and his father said only, "You're asking me which ones I'd keep."

"I already picked. I'm asking if you'd have picked the same."

His father looked a long time. The bulb swung a little in the draft from the open door. Then he pointed at the hands, black to the wrist.

"That one's mine," he said. "The rest are yours."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In a 2014 study led by David Yeager, students were more likely to revise essays when critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them.
story:
I have never been the kind of person who says things behind people's backs, which is exactly why I was standing in Ayana's kitchen holding a warm soda and trying to figure out how to say something to Aliza's face. The party was her eighteenth birthday, her actual birthday, and the whole senior class seemed to have funneled into this one narrow house with its paper lanterns and a playlist that somebody's little brother kept hijacking. Aliza was by the sliding glass door, laughing at something, holding the third draft of the personal essay we had agreed to swap before graduation. She had already read mine. She had said, in her tidy handwriting, "I don't buy the ending. It resolves too neatly, like you got tired." That note had stung for two days and then made the essay better, and I still had not returned the favor.

"I'm not avoiding her," I told Ayana, who was stacking cups at the counter and not pretending to believe me. Ayana had watched me carry Aliza's draft to three separate corners of the party like a man transporting contraband.

"You've read it eight times," she said. "In front of me. You read it twice during the cake."

The truth, which I was arranging carefully in my head so it would arrive in a shape that could not be blamed on me, was that the essay was about her brother's accident and it fell apart in the middle. The first half was brave, specific, alive. Then it got vague and safe, the way writing does when the writer stops trusting the reader, and the last paragraph was a greeting card. I knew that. I had circled it in pencil and then erased the circles, because Aliza had cried the last time a coach critiqued her, and because I was, I kept telling myself, a kind person.

Ms. Martínez had assigned us as writing partners in the fall, and in December she had read us something from a study, a 2014 study led by David Yeager, about how students were more likely to revise their essays when the teacher's critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed the student could meet them. I had half tuned it out, because Ms. Martínez explained things with her whole body and it was last period. But the sentence had stayed with me the way certain amalgams of luck and weather stay with you, half one thing and half another, indistinct but heavy. Criticism plus belief equaled revision. Criticism alone equaled a draft shoved into a folder. It was not a complicated formula, though I had spent three months failing to apply it.

The problem was that belief was the hard part. Sarcasm, deflection, false praise, those came to me like something atavistic, older than language. Kindness with a real spine in it had to be built on purpose.

Aliza caught my eye across the room and held up her cup, and I walked over before I could complete my retreat to the porch. "You've got my essay and that face," she said. "The face you make when you're about to pathologize someone's comma placement."

"It's not commas." I put the draft on the windowsill between us, where the lantern light caught the eraser ghosts of my circles. "First, though, I have to say something, and you're going to think it's a trick, and it's not. The first half of this is the best thing anyone in our class wrote this year. I mean that. So when I tell you the middle falls apart, you have to believe I'm saying it because I think you can fix it, not because I want it fixed. High standards. That's the whole sentence."

"That's two sentences."

"It's a belief system," I said. "The middle, where you go from the hospital to the part about lessons learned. You skip the night you actually found out. You skip all of it, and then the ending forgives everybody, and I don't think you've forgiven anybody yet."

She looked at the paper for a long time. The music changed to something her brother had probably chosen. "The night we found out," she said quietly, "my mom drove through three red lights. I've never written that down."

"Write it down."

She folded the draft and put it in her back pocket instead of her bag, which for some reason felt like the more serious commitment. Then she said, "You know I never read your essay past the second page, right? I wrote that note about the ending without finishing it. You actually wrapped it up fine. I just assumed you'd gotten tired, because you always get tired."

Ayana, passing with the cake knife, smiled at the ceiling.

I stood there holding my honest, specific, deeply principled feedback, and watched Aliza walk outside to start, I think, her fourth draft. "So the last page was fine," I said to nobody.

"Best thing anyone in our class wrote this year," Ayana said, and handed me a fork.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Carryover cooking means food keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, and a large roast's internal temperature can rise by several degrees while it rests.
story:
John had promised his mother a proper dinner on the second night at the campsite, partly because he wanted to and partly because she had threatened, with a smile that was only sixty percent a smile, to survive on granola bars forever if he didn't. The cooler held a large pork roast, a birthday gift of ambition from his own earlier self, and he crouched over the charcoal grill at six in the evening, poking at the coals with a stick like a man defusing something. Kelsey and Lacey had wandered over from the next campsite to watch, which he suspected was less about companionship and more about entertainment.

"Are you going to poke it or cook it?" Lacey asked, sitting on the picnic table with her ankles crossed.

"Both," John said. "Poking catalyzes the coals."

"That is not what catalyzes means," said Kelsey, who had finished AP Chem and mentioned it whenever possible.

"It is what it means when I do it."

He had studied the roast that afternoon with the seriousness of a scholar, one hand on his phone, and had landed on a number: one hundred forty-five degrees, pulled from the heat, safe and juicy. He'd found the thermometer in the kitchen bin his father had packed, a bin that otherwise contained three kinds of mustard and a single egg. When the roast finally hit one hundred forty-five, golden and crackling, he lifted it off with a hero's confidence and set it on the cutting board to rest, exactly as the article had instructed, while he went to find the plates.

Ten minutes later he carved it, and the center was gray, the juices gone thin and sad into the board's grooves. He stood there with the knife in his hand, genuinely betrayed. His father tasted a slice and said nothing, which was worse than saying something. Lacey said, "It's not terrible," in the voice people use for things that are terrible. John cut another slice, stared into it like a cave, and carried his phone down to the lake so he could think without an audience of politely chewing faces.

From Kelsey's spot at the table, watching him walk off with his shoulders up around his ears, the whole thing looked almost funny, though she kept that to herself. She liked that John took cooking so seriously that failure actually wounded him; most guys their age considered a sandwich an achievement. She finished her gray slice anyway, because she was hungry and because the crust really was good, and she watched John's mother quietly slide a second roast, the backup, out of the cooler, as if she had always known this might be necessary. "Your mom's the real strategist," she said to Lacey. "She packed a contingency roast."

John came back from the lake with a strange expression, somewhere between defeat and discovery. He held up the phone. "It's called carryover cooking," he said. "It keeps cooking after it leaves the heat. A big roast like this, the temperature can go up several degrees while it rests."

"So it overshot," his father said.

"It overshot. I took it out at one hundred forty-five and it just kept going without me." He said it like a man describing a girlfriend who had left with the car. Then he circumspectly turned the backup roast over in his hands, checking it from every angle, as if it might be hiding a second betrayal, and repositioned the coals with a care that made even Lacey stop chewing to watch.

He pulled the second roast at one hundred thirty-eight degrees, five minutes before his mother would have, and everyone at the table had opinions about that. Lacey thought it was reckless; Kelsey argued that it was the rational move given the evidence; Mr. Tanaka, the retired teacher from the far campsite who had drifted over following the smell, said only, "The boy trusts the physics," and helped himself to a chair. John did not explain himself, partly because he wasn't fully sure, partly because explaining would have sounded like bragging, and the roast sat there under foil while they all waited, none of them entirely certain whether they were about to eat perfection or undercook something expensive.

When he carved it, fifteen minutes later, the meat was faintly pink, the juices pooled bright in the slices, and Mr. Tanaka took the first bite before anyone else could. He chewed. He looked at the lake for a while.

"Well?" said Lacey.

"Give it a moment," Mr. Tanaka said, and reached for another slice.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: The US federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009, though many states and cities set a higher minimum.
story:
Alex got the job because he was the only applicant who showed up in a collared shirt, which he suspected was also why they offered him seven twenty-five an hour and called it standard. The camp sat at the edge of a park in one state, and the swimming lake everyone used sat just over the line in the other, so that lunch counts and head counts happened under two different governments without anyone remarking on it. His job was to carry the first-aid kit, count heads, and stand in the shallow water while eight-year-olds attempted to drown each other with pool noodles.

On the second Friday, paychecks arrived in thin envelopes, and Hussain tore his open on the bus bench while Brendon leaned over his shoulder. Hussain had spent the summer across the lake, leading kayaking for a camp whose director, Ms. Nkosi, was famous for paying well and for firing anyone who texted during a swim test. He read his number aloud, then read it again, as though the print might revise itself downward.

"That's per day, right," Brendon said. "Not per hour."

"Per hour."

Alex did the arithmetic on the back of his own envelope, where his hourly figure sat in patient small type. Hussain was making nearly three dollars more per hour for what looked, from the shore, like the same job: whistle, sunscreen, children. Brendon, who worked at the ice cream stand and was paid in cash and leftovers, declared the whole thing a scam and demanded to know who to call.

"Nobody scammed you," Hussain said. "It's just different. Ms. Nkosi says the federal minimum's been seven twenty-five since July 24, 2009, and our state sets it higher, and the camp can't go under the state number. Your camp apparently can." He said it the way he reported scores, without editorial.

Alex had assumed, in the way he assumed about gravity and grades, that there was one number, posted somewhere official, that everyone paid. The idea that the country had a floor that hadn't moved since he was three years old, and that whole states simply built their own floors on top of it, rearranged something in his head. He did not yet know what to do with the rearrangement. It was not exactly unfair, since he had agreed to the seven twenty-five, and it was not exactly fair, since he had agreed the way you agree to a price written on a sign, believing the sign had been checked by somebody.

He walked home along the lake road, turning it over. His father would say the answer was to ask for more, calmly, with a reason. Hussain would say the answer was to quit and work for Ms. Nkosi, except that her kayaking slots had filled in April. Brendon would say the answer was to organize the noodle children into a union, which was a joke and also, Alex thought, not entirely one. Each of them was parochial in his own direction, seeing the whole question from inside his own paycheck, and Alex could feel himself doing it too, taking his envelope as the measure of the world.

On Monday he asked Ms. Nkosi, who had come across the lake for the weekly supply run, whether she had openings. She looked at him over the tailgate of her van.

"I have one," she said. "Equipment shed. You'd inventory paddles and alphabetize the first-aid supplies for minimum, my minimum. It's boring and it's honest work."

"It's more than I make watching children try to kill each other with foam."

She almost smiled. "Then take it. But tell me you're not coming just for the number."

He considered lying, then considered that she would know. "Partly for the number," he said. "Partly because I'd rather find out how your camp works than keep wondering why ours works the way it does." He heard his own pedantry and flinched at it, and she did not flinch at all.

He gave notice at his camp that afternoon, and the director said he'd transfigure back into a counselor if he ever changed his mind, which Alex took to mean the man had looked up the word that morning. He carried the first-aid kit one last time, stood in the shallows while the noodle war raged, and counted eight heads. Then he waded out, held up his whistle, and shouted, "Same time tomorrow, but I won't be here."

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: In the Jewish Passover tradition, the festive meal is called a Seder, a Hebrew word meaning 'order', because its rituals follow a fixed sequence from start to finish.
story:
The practice Haggadahs were stacked on a table at the back of the synagogue library, and Benjamin had been staring at them for a full minute before Flora nudged his elbow. "You can read them, you know," she said. "They're not going to bite."

He took the top copy and opened it at random, somewhere in the middle, where the pages were a chaos of Hebrew, English instructions, and small florid illustrations of matzah and wine cups. His grandfather had led the family Seder every year of Benjamin's life, sitting at the head of his sister's dining room table with a cup that never seemed to empty. This year his grandfather was in a hospital bed on the far side of the city, too tired for visitors longer than twenty minutes, and at the last visit he had gripped Benjamin's wrist and said, "You'll do it. You know the tunes." Benjamin had said yes before he had any idea what he was agreeing to.

"They're running this class because half the kids our age can't tell Kiddush from Karpas," Vance said, dropping into the chair beside Flora. He flipped his Haggadah upside down as a joke, then righted it. Vance's family belonged to a different congregation, but he'd come anyway, claiming it was for the free grape juice. Benjamin suspected it was because Flora had come.

Ms. Joshi, who ran the library and had organized the evening, set a timer on the table. "An hour," she said. "Lead each other through it, start to finish. Switch leaders halfway." She did not sit down with them, which Benjamin understood as intentional. She was not going to teach it to him. She was going to make him teach it to himself.

He began at the first page, and for a while it went well: the blessing, the first cup, everyone stealing glances at each other to check whether they were washing their hands right. Then Flora asked for more grape juice, and Vance told a story about his cousin hiding the afikoman in the light fixture one year and forgetting it there, and by the time Benjamin found his place again, the page looked unfamiliar. Had they said the blessing over the vegetable or not? He turned back one page, then forward two, his thumb keeping a place he was no longer sure was the right one. Flora watched him do it and said nothing, which was somehow worse than if she'd laughed.

"It's called a Seder because it means 'order'," Vance said, when Benjamin finally admitted he'd lost the thread. "My rabbi drilled that into us. The whole meal runs in a fixed sequence, first step to last. That's the whole point of the name."

Benjamin looked down at the book in his lap. He had said the word Seder a thousand times without once holding still to look at it. His grandfather had never used a list, never flipped pages in confusion; he simply rose through the meal as if it were a staircase he'd climbed so many times his feet knew it in the dark. Benjamin had always assumed that came from being old. Now he understood it came from somewhere else, from years of carrying it, and he thought about his own yes at the hospital, given so quickly, and how much certainty he had spent in that one syllable. Whether it had been courage or just not thinking first, he couldn't yet say.

He tore a strip from the margin of the synagogue's announcement flyer, folded it into quarters, and wrote the steps on it in pencil, numbered, one through fifteen, in the order the Haggadah laid them out. When they reached the halfway point Ms. Joshi had set, he handed the strip to Flora and made her lead, so he could feel the shape of it from the follower's side too, where his grandfather must have sat once, decades ago, before anyone thought of him as the one at the head of the table.

The timer went off just as they poured the third cup, which was only juice, which was somehow still festive. Ms. Joshi collected the Haggadahs, and Benjamin kept the pencil strip, folding it small and pressing it into his pocket.

"Think you can do it Thursday?" Flora asked, shrugging into her coat.

"I can do it in order," Benjamin said. "Everything after that, I'll find out."

Vance held the door, and the three of them walked out into the parking lot, where the streetlights had just come on, transfixing the last pale edge of snow in a row of orange stripes. Flora asked if he was nervous, and Benjamin patted his pocket where the folded list sat, and said, "Ask me after the fourth question."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Kintsugi is a Japanese technique of repairing broken pottery with lacquer mixed or dusted with powdered gold, treating the break as part of the object's history rather than hiding it.
story:
The bowl had been her grandmother's, and Rosalie had broken it on a Tuesday, carrying it to the table to photograph it for an art assignment about inherited objects. Now, four days later, she sat at the kitchen table with the pieces laid out on a dish towel like evidence, and a browser tab open on her laptop that she had not closed since midnight. The tab was about kintsugi. She had typed "repair broken pottery gold" into the search bar expecting glue and paint, and what came back had captivated her so completely that she had read the same paragraph six times.

"It's called kintsugi," she said aloud that afternoon, testing it, when Eliana came over with two iced coffees and found her still there, still in yesterday's sweatshirt. "This Japanese technique. You repair the broken pottery with lacquer mixed with gold dust, actual powdered gold, and you don't hide the crack. You make it part of the thing."

Eliana pulled out the chair across from her and set a coffee down within reach, which was as close as she got to sympathy. "So you broke your grandmother's bowl and your plan is to make it worse-looking on purpose."

"Better-looking," Rosalie said. "It treats the break as part of the bowl's history. That's the whole point. It's not pretending nothing happened." She turned one of the shards with her fingertip. The glaze inside was a blue so dark it read as black, and the broken edge was rough and pale, like bread.

Her mother still didn't know. Rosalie had wrapped the pieces in the dish towel and carried them upstairs the night it happened, and every dinner since had been a small exercise in not looking at the cabinet where the bowl lived between uses. Her mother was mercurial about objects; she could laugh off a totaled car and then go quiet for two days over a chipped mug, and Rosalie could never predict which version she would get. Her grandmother, who had owned the bowl first and had been dead for three years, would have been the easier confession. Her grandmother had dropped things herself, cheerfully, all the time.

"The problem is the gold," Eliana said, scrolling through the tab. "It says dusted or mixed into lacquer. Where are you getting powdered gold? You have twelve dollars."

"I was thinking Mr. Morningstar." Their neighbor taught shop at the middle school and kept a garage full of things people should not keep, soldering irons and cigar boxes of watch parts. Rosalie had seen, once, a small jar of gold-colored powder on his shelf next to the clock springs, and had never asked about it because she'd had no reason to. Now she had a reason. Eliana pointed out that it was probably just brass, and Rosalie said that she would rather know than guess, which was, Eliana noted, a new policy for her.

Mr. Morningstar turned the jar in his hands when she asked, squinting at the label worn down to nothing.
