He said it was gilt powder from an old frame restoration, and he gave it to her on the condition that she come back and show him what she made, because he liked seeing what people made. He did not ask whose bowl it was. He did say, as she reached the gate, that in his experience the second break was the one that ruined a thing, so she should take her time. She had stood in the driveway holding the jar against her stomach like something warm.

At the kitchen table she practiced first, on a mug she found at the back of a cupboard, its handle long since gone. Her first attempt was a travesty, glue everywhere, the powder clumping into a dull seam that looked like a scar a child would draw. She scraped it off, ruined the mug entirely, and started again on a saucer with cleaner edges, and the second time the line came out thin and bright, and she sat with her chin almost on the table, just looking at it. There was a part of her that understood the appeal immediately, and a part that kept arguing. The bowl had been perfect before her. Her grandmother had bought it whole. Was a repaired bowl the same bowl, or a new one that had eaten the old one? She did not know, and she noticed that not knowing had stopped feeling like an emergency.

She worked on the real pieces after her mother went to bed, breath shallow, following the old seams. When she finished, near one in the morning, she set the bowl in the center of the kitchen table and turned off every light except the one above the stove. The gold caught that weak orange light and held it, a lightning-shaped vein running blue to rim. In the morning her mother would come down and see it, and Rosalie would be asleep, or pretending to be, and whichever version of her mother walked into the kitchen would find the bowl whole and broken at once, its history visible, not hidden. Rosalie touched the seam once, lightly, with one finger.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Malcolm Gladwell's 2008 book Outliers popularized the '10,000-hour rule', though Ericsson later said the quality of practice matters more than any fixed number of hours.
story:
Ashleigh said it in the parking lot, zipping her trumpet case shut with the finality of a judge. "It's pointless starting guitar at seventeen. You need ten thousand hours, and by the time you have them you'll be thirty." Henry, who had turned sixteen in March and had his first lesson booked for Saturday, said nothing on the drive home, but that night he looked it up and found the source: Malcolm Gladwell's 2008 book Outliers, which had popularized the so-called ten-thousand-hour rule. Ten thousand hours. He did the math twice on the back of a chemistry worksheet. Three hours a day for nine years. He lay on his bed with his putative future rearranging itself above him, a whole imagined life in which he was always behind.

Ms. Rodríguez's studio occupied the back room of a house on Alder Street, carpeted in a way that swallowed sound, with a metronome shaped like a pyramid and a rubber plant that had clearly given up. She was tuning a loaner guitar when he arrived, and she let him sit and hold it before she asked him anything. His fingers went where she showed them, clumsy on the nylon strings, and when he pressed too hard a note bent flat like a small apology.

"You're counting already," she said, mid-lesson, watching his eyes drift to the clock. "I can see arithmetic happening behind your face."

He told her, because it was easier than carrying it. The ten thousand hours, the friend's verdict, the fact that Gladwell had gotten it from somewhere, some researcher, he couldn't remember the name. Ms. Rodríguez didn't deliver a speech. She said, "Play the E chord again," and then, "again," and then, "now notice your wrist," and by the time he'd done it forty times his left hand ached in a way that felt weirdly like progress.

Christophe found the rest of it, because Christophe read everything and remembered worse things. They were in the library Tuesday, Christophe ostensibly studying stagflation for economics, actually reading about a collapsed football league. "It's Ericsson," he said, spinning the laptop around. "The researcher. Ericsson later said the quality of practice matters more than any fixed number of hours." He read it aloud like a weather report. "So Ashleigh's math is real but the rule is soft. It's like she quoted the trailer instead of the film."

"Is that supposed to be encouraging?"

"It's supposed to be accurate. Encouraging is above my pay grade." Christophe went back to stagflation, muttering about oil prices and the seventies, and Henry copied the sentence into his phone. He didn't feel solved. The number was still the number, and Ericsson hadn't said hours didn't matter, only that quality counted for more, and what did quality even mean, and how would he know if his practice had it? He sat with both ideas the way you hold two groceries in one hand, unwilling to set either down.

Saturday he told Ms. Rodríguez the whole thing while she recuperated from a cold, tea steaming on the windowsill, her voice reduced to a rasp. He said he'd started thinking the hours were a wall, then a doorway, and now he thought it was more like neither, more like a map that left out the terrain. She listened with her chin on her hand. "So what do you want to do about it?" she rasped, and when he didn't answer, she reached over and slid the capo up the neck of his guitar. "Play it here. Same chord. Tell me what changes."

He played it. The same shape sounded higher, brighter, suddenly a different animal, and he played it again, and then the E after it, and heard for the first time that the E was slightly dead because his third finger was resting against the string below. A small flaw he'd been carrying for two weeks without noticing. He fixed it, and the chord rang clean, and something in his chest unlocked a single notch. It was one note, fixed, in a carpeted room. It was not ten thousand of anything. It might, he thought, be the kind of thing that counted for more.

He texted Ashleigh from the bus: your rule has a footnote. She replied with a single question mark, then, five minutes later, an admission that she'd gotten it from her cousin. He put the phone away and looked out the window at the shuttered bakery on Alder, the bus shelter with its peeling ad for a band that had broken up. He still didn't know if he'd be any good. He knew the shape of an E chord, and where his third finger belonged, and that next Saturday the rubber plant would still be dying and Ms. Rodríguez would still say, before anything else, "Play it again."

At home he practiced until his fingertips went tender, stopped, soaked them in cold water, and started over.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: To indemnify someone is to promise, in a contract, to compensate them for losses they suffer because of certain acts, often written alongside a promise to 'hold harmless'.
story:
The queue at the bank moved in lurches, and Carson counted the people ahead of him twice, both times getting five, which felt like a bad omen for someone about to do arithmetic with money. In his backpack were two documents: a student account form his mother had signed, and the rental agreement for the Legion hall, which Rowan had shoved at him that morning with the words "you're the responsible one, it's basically your brand." The second document was unsigned, and unsigned, as far as Carson could tell, meant the show on Saturday did not exist.

Rowan had come along ostensibly for company and actually for the free lollipops by the teller counter. He stood at the little display now, rattling the bowl like a maraca. "These are autochthonous to this counter," he said. "Born here, die here, never see the outside world. A lollipop's whole life in one branch office."

"Stop eating the inventory."

"It's not inventory, it's hospitality." He unwrapped a green one anyway.

When Carson's number came up, the counter clerk stamped his account form, scanned his mother's signature, and slid a temporary card across the glass with the ceremony of someone handing over a passport. "You can deposit today. The card activates in the morning." That was the easy half done. Money could now enter Carson's possession, theoretically, if anyone bought tickets.

The hard half was still in his bag. The Legion hall wanted four hundred dollars, a damage deposit, and a signature on a page that Carson had read three times the night before, and the sentence he kept returning to was this: "The renter agrees to indemnify and hold harmless the Legion against all claims arising from the event." He laid the rental form on the counter, next to the student paperwork, the two documents side by side like before and after photographs.

"I have a question," he said. "About a word."

The clerk called someone over, and the someone turned out to be Mr. Rahimi, who coached junior soccer two streets from Carson's house and who apparently also processed small-business accounts on weekdays. He read the sentence with his lips barely moving, the way he read offside rulings. "You're renting the hall for what?"

"A show. Bands. Ticketed, sort of." The word "sort of" did a lot of work in that sentence, and Mr. Rahimi's eyebrows registered the load.

"Who signs this? You?"

"I'm sixteen," Carson said, and even to himself it sounded less like an answer than like a defense.

Rowan had drifted over, lollipop stick jutting from his mouth like a cigarette in an old movie, and he pulled out his phone before Mr. Rahimi could say anything. "Hang on, I looked this up last night." He scrolled, stopped, read aloud. "To indemnify someone is to promise, in a contract, to compensate them for losses they suffer because of certain acts." He scrolled again. "And it usually gets written next to 'hold harmless,' like right here, see, both of them, together."

"Thank you," said Mr. Rahimi, in the flat tone of a man who had been about to say exactly that.

"So if somebody trips over a speaker cable and cracks their head open," Carson said slowly, "and sues the Legion, we pay the Legion back. For their losses. Because of our show."

"Because of certain acts," Rowan agreed cheerfully, as if the phrase were a fun accessory and not a cliff.

The air near the counter felt strange, statically charged, the way the copier room at school could ionize on a dry day, so that the hairs on Carson's forearm lifted and settled. Or maybe it was just him. His father's voice was in one ear, the one that said never sign what you don't understand, and Rowan's whole philosophy was in the other, which held that everyone signed everything all the time, phone updates, gym memberships, field trip forms, and civilization had not yet collapsed. Both could not be right. Both might not be wrong, either. The truth, Carson suspected, lived in the space between: signatures were cheap until they weren't, and the only way to tell was to read every clause and then decide which risks you actually believed in.

"Here's the thing," he said. "I can't sign this anyway. I'm a minor. My mom has to sign, and she'll read it, and she'll ask me what indemnify means, and last week I would have said no idea." He squared the two forms, account beneath rental, and put them both back in the bag. "Can I take one of these deposit slips for the venue? They want a certified cheque."

Mr. Rahimi produced the slip. "Bring your mother in before Saturday," he said. "And get insurance on the equipment if you can."

"It's Loick's equipment," said Rowan. "Loick's amp, Loick's PA. He'd rather die than let anyone touch it."

"Then Loick should read page two," said Mr. Rahimi, "where it says the renter is liable for damage to the premises."

Rowan's lollipop stopped mid-rotation. "Page two?"

"There's a page two?"

On the walk out, Carson texted Loick a photo of page two and then, before the typing dots could appear, a second message: meet us at my house, my mom's home at five.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: Charoset, a sweet paste of chopped fruit and nuts on the Seder plate, represents the mortar the enslaved Israelites used to lay bricks in Egypt.
story:
The synagogue kitchen smelled of apples and walnuts on the Thursday before Passover, and Jake stood at the steel counter with a cutting board, a paring knife, and the uneasy awareness that twelve people were expecting him to run the Seder on Saturday night. His grandfather had led it every year since before Jake was born, and this winter his grandfather's hands had begun to shake too much to lift the cup. Nobody had said anything directly. His mother had simply slid the Haggadah across the table one Sunday and looked at him.

Mr. Sinclair, who taught the b'nai mitzvah students and ran the kitchen on rehearsal nights, had put out the ingredients without commentary: apples, walnuts, raisins, a jar of Manischewitz, a lemon. "You're leading, so you make it," he said, and went to check on the oven. That was his method, Jake had learned. He arranged the pieces and then removed himself.

Meghan and Leonidas were there for the same reason, each of them someday expected to lead a table of their own. Meghan had taken the horseradish root and was scraping at it with the peeler, wincing. Leonidas had the job of separating eggs for the soup, and he kept glancing at his phone between each one, which meant he cracked them badly and fished out shell fragments with a fingertip. The window over the sink faced the back lawn, where the winter grass had gone pale and flat, a small brown savanna under the floodlights.

Jake chopped the apples small, then smaller, then too small, and started over. When he mixed in the nuts and wine, the paste came together dark and grainy, and he set it in the bowl Leonidas pushed toward him. Meghan leaned over it, breathing in through her nose. "Okay, but what is it? Like, what's it for?" She dipped a spoon in without asking. "Because honestly it just tastes like sweet stuff."

Jake opened his mouth and found nothing in it. He knew where it sat on the Seder plate, between the parsley and the shank bone, and he knew his grandfather spooned it generously and made a joke about cholesterol. He knew he liked it. That was the whole inventory. He stood there with his wooden spoon raised while the sound of the oven fan filled the silence, and Meghan watched him not answer.

"It's charoset," he said finally, which was a name, not an answer. He pulled the Haggadah toward him across the counter, past the wine stains of other years, and turned pages with a sticky thumb until he found the commentary in the margin, small print he had never once read. He read it twice, because the first time it seemed like it had to be a mistake. Then he read it aloud. "Charoset is the mortar. The mortar the enslaved Israelites used to lay bricks in Egypt." He looked up. Meghan had stopped chewing. "The sweet stuff," he said. "It's mortar."

"It's delicious mortar," Leonidas said from the stove, but he said it quietly, and he put the phone face down on the counter.

Jake carried the bowl to the Seder plate that Mr. Sinclair had set out for practice, an old tin one with flaking paint, and he placed the charoset in its section and stood looking at the arrangement. There was parsley for spring, salt water for tears, a bone, an egg, and now this: sweetness standing in for the mud of forced labor. He had always thought of the Seder as a performance you got through, the same songs in the same order, his uncle falling asleep by the second cup. But the plate was doing something else. It took the story and externalized it, put it where hands could reach it, where a spoon could carry slavery into your actual mouth. He didn't know yet what to do with that, and he was honest enough with himself to admit it. He was eighteen, and mortar tasted like apples, and both of those things were true at once.

Saturday night, his grandfather sat at the table with his shaking hands folded and his eyes on Jake. Jake poured the first cup, lifted it, said the blessing over the wine in a voice that surprised him by staying level. His little cousins squirmed. His mother watched from the kitchen doorway with a dish towel over her shoulder. When they reached the Seder plate, Jake picked up the charoset bowl before anyone could prompt him.

"This," he said, holding it up, "is the mortar the enslaved Israelites used to lay bricks in Egypt." He spooned some onto his grandfather's matzah himself, a thick layer, the way his grandfather had always done it for everyone else. His grandfather looked at the matzah, then at him, and nodded once.

"Eat your mortar," his grandfather said, and the table laughed, and Jake passed the bowl to his left.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Spanish news writers often attribute a claim with 'según', meaning 'according to', which tells a reader the statement comes from a source, not the reporter.
story:
Sydney spread the newspaper across her grandmother's kitchen table, smoothing the crease where it had been folded for two days. The article was short, four paragraphs about a drought in the south of Spain, and her assignment was just as short: read it aloud, then summarise it in her own words for Monday's class. Spanish Three had seemed manageable in September. Now, in her grandmother's house with the October light slanting through the lace curtains, she wondered why she had ever believed that.

"Abuela," she said, "did you get newspapers like this, when you were little?"

Her grandmother set down the dish towel and came to look. "Every morning. My father read them cover to cover." She tapped the headline with one finger. "You can do this. Take it slow."

That was the problem. Sydney could not take it slow enough. The first paragraph went all right, words she recognized, reservoirs and rain and a region she found on the map app under the table. But the second paragraph stopped her cold. It said, near as she could tell, that the reservoirs would run dry by spring. Flat. Certain. Like a fact the paper itself was stating, and she wrote that down in her summary draft and felt uneasy about it all through lunch.

After lunch she texted Maximus, who was in her class and had been her nemesis since the eighth grade spelling bee, when he had won on the word "ricochet" after she missed it. He was insufferable about that for a full year. But he was also good at Spanish, better than she was, and she swallowed her pride and sent him a photo of the paragraph with a question mark.

His reply came while she was washing the lunch dishes. "look at the second word," he wrote. She dried her hands, dripped water on the newsprint, and looked. "Según," he'd circled it in the photo. "It means 'according to.'"

Sydney sat back down and cogitated on that for a while, chin on her fist, the paper damp under her fingers. According to. According to whom? She found the answer a clause later: according to the water agency, according to a farmers' association. The claim about the reservoirs running dry was not the newspaper's claim at all. It was somebody's statement, attributed, passed along with a small word doing the heavy lifting. She scrolled back through the article and found "según" twice more, each time handing a claim to a named source like a baton in a relay. The reporter, she realized, never once said the reservoirs would run dry. The reporter only said that other people said so.

Her grandmother brought her coffee with too much milk in it, the way she drank it at sixteen, and sat down across from her. "You look like you solved something."

"Sort of." Sydney turned the paper around. "This sentence, I thought it was a fact. Like the paper was promising it. But it's not. It's según somebody. The reporter's just telling us who said it."

Her grandmother smiled at the word as if it were an old acquaintance. "That's how careful people talk," she said. "You watch, in any language. The careful ones always tell you who told them."

Sydney practiced the summary out loud four times, first to the kitchen, then to her grandmother, who listened with her hands folded and corrected nothing because she could not, and finally to Ariane over video call, since Ariane would be in Monday's audience. "Better," Ariane said. "But you still say it like the drought thing is guaranteed. Say who claims it."

"According to the water agency, reservoirs could be critical by spring," Sydney said, and heard the difference herself, the small door the phrase opened, the daylight between what was known and what was asserted. She was honest with herself about what she still could not tell: whether the agency was right, whether the farmers were exaggerating, whether the whole thing was more or less dire than the article made it seem. The word "según" told her where a claim came from. It did not tell her whether to believe it, and she thought, briefly, that this might be deleterious to her grade, summarizing with all those hedges, if Mr. Kowalski wanted clean confident sentences. She decided he would have to live with the hedges.

On Monday morning Mr. Kowalski called on her second, right after Maximus, who read smoothly and summarized even more smoothly, every claim flat and unattributed, the reporter's voice and the sources' voices mashed together. When Sydney finished her own turn, she made sure to say "according to the water agency" and "according to the farmers' association" out loud, twice each, and she saw Maximus, three rows over, look down at his paper and start circling something with his pen.

After class he caught her at the door. "Hey," he said. "That según thing. Was that in the article or did you make that up?"

"It's in the article," she said. "Look at the second word."

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: The STAR method answers interview questions about past behavior by describing a Situation, the Task required, the Action you took, and the Result.
story:
The application had been sitting in Eve's backpack for six days, creased once where the water bottle pressed against it. It was for a barista position at the coffee shop on Marsh Street, the one with the green awning that she passed every morning on her way to the day camp where she'd volunteered for the last two summers. Mr. Tse, who ran the camp, had told her in June that she should get paid for something, that volunteering was lovely but rent was real, and she had laughed and then gone home and looked up the word "ascetic" because Logan had used it to describe her, and she hadn't liked the dictionary's confirmation.

"So what do I even say to them?" she asked Gwendolyn on Thursday, the two of them sitting on the overturned canoe behind the camp's boathouse while eleven-year-olds shrieked somewhere down the shore. "They'll ask about experience and I have exactly none. I have a lanyard and a whistle."

Gwendolyn, who had worked at a garden centre the previous summer and therefore spoke with the authority of the previously employed, tore a strip off her granola bar wrapper. "They don't care about experience for the coffee one. My cousin said they ask stuff like, tell me about a time something went wrong. You have to have a story ready."

"Something always goes wrong here," Eve said. "Yesterday a kid put a frog in the first aid kit."

"That's not a story, that's an anecdote. You have to structure it." Gwendolyn frowned at the lake as though the structure were floating somewhere near the buoys. "My cousin called it something. STAR? She said it answers interview questions about past behavior. You describe the Situation, then the Task, then the Action you took, and the Result. Four things."

"Like a recipe."

"Like a recipe," Gwendolyn agreed, and then a counselor whistled and they both stood up and brushed sand off the backs of their legs.

Eve practiced that night in the bathroom mirror, which felt ridiculous, so she stopped doing the mirror and just talked to the shower curtain. The story she chose was the group project from spring: the mural for the library, when two of her teammates had stopped showing up and the paint order had come in wrong and she had, at the eleventh hour, redrawn the design at half scale so they could finish on the wall they actually had. Situation, task, action, result. Saying it in order made her feel slightly fraudulent, as if she were narrating her own life in the third person, but she noticed something else too: when she followed the shape, she stopped rambling. The four parts were like handholds on a climbing wall. She got through the whole account in ninety seconds and it had an ending.

The interview was Saturday at ten. Eve wore the one blouse she owned and arrived nine minutes early, which she then had to contextualize for herself, sitting in the window seat with a glass of water, so that it read as diligence rather than desperation. The manager was younger than she'd expected, maybe twenty-five, with a pen behind her ear. "Tell me about a time you worked with a group and it didn't go smoothly," she said, four minutes in, and Eve's mind went briefly and completely white, and then the handholds appeared.

"The mural at the public library," she began. The situation: a team of five, a deadline, a wall half the size they'd been promised. The task: finish on time anyway, or the library took the grant money back. Her action: she called a meeting nobody wanted to attend, cut the design down, reassigned the two who'd gone quiet to prep work they could do alone. The result: they finished a day early, and the librarian asked them back for the children's wing. She heard herself say all four parts and heard them hold together, and when she stopped talking the manager was writing something down, which Eve chose to believe was a good sign.

From where the manager sat, the girl across the table looked nervous in the first minute and then suddenly not, like someone who had rehearsed exactly this and was now trying to seem unrehearsed. She liked that. Most applicants her age either froze or talked for six uninterrupted minutes about how much they loved coffee. This one had a shape to her answer, a beginning and an end, and when asked what she'd do differently she didn't say "nothing," which everyone said and nobody meant. She said, "I'd check the wall measurements myself in the first week instead of trusting the email," and then, after a pause, "I'm still not sure the smaller design was better. It was just possible." That pause was worth more than the answer.

Eve got the call on Tuesday, during lunch duty, and had to walk behind the storage shed to hear it over the sound of forty children eating. She took the job. She would start in August, mornings before camp, which meant giving up the sleep she'd been treating as a summer entitlement, and she stood behind the shed a moment longer holding the phone against her chest, not yet sure whether what she felt was triumph or the small grief of a schedule becoming fixed.

That evening she found Mr. Tse locking the equipment shed. "I got the job," she said. "The coffee place."

"Congratulations. First real paycheque." He jingled the padlock.

"I lied a little," she said. "In the interview. Not lied. I told the mural story in this rehearsed way, and it worked, and I don't know if it worked because the story was true or because the shape was good." She picked up a pebble and threw it at the shed door, badly.

Mr. Tse considered her for a moment. "You'll figure out which part mattered the first time something spills," he said, and handed her his keys to lock up.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: GIS layers stored in different coordinate reference systems will not line up correctly until one is reprojected to match the other.
story:
The departures board flipped from delayed to delayed again, and Alexandre unfolded his laptop on the cold metal armrest because there was nothing else to do with three hours and a gate full of strangers. Ms. Shin had taken the row of seats nearest the window and was watching the lightning stack up over the tarmac, so he angled his screen toward her too, the way he did when he wanted a witness without asking for one. Santino dropped into the seat on his other side with two sodas and a bag of pretzels he had no intention of sharing. "You're seriously doing homework," Santino said. "We're trapped in an airport during the apocalypse."

"It's due Monday whether we fly or not." Alexandre opened the two files Ms. Shin had sent the class before they left, the flood risk layer and the housing layer, the two halves of the project she had assigned about which neighborhoods in their city actually sat in the water's path. He had been drawn to it in a way he couldn't quite defend, the way certain maps had captivated him since he was small, when he used to trace the bus routes on the folded paper map his father kept in the glove box, running his finger along the lines until he had them memorized.

He clicked the overlay button and the two maps merged, and there was the river, fat and blue, running directly through the middle of city hall. Santino leaned over, chewing, and said, "Since when is there a river downtown?" Tyrone, sulking two seats down with his headphones around his neck like a collar, pulled one ear free and said, "There isn't. That's the point of a downtown."

Alexandre dragged the layers apart and put them back together and the river stayed where it was, slicing through the courthouse, through the school administration building, through a parking structure that had stood dry for forty years. He checked the housing layer alone and it looked right, streets where the streets were. He checked the flood layer alone and it looked right too. Together they were wrong, and the wrongness was so complete it had to mean something, though he couldn't yet say what.

Tyrone came over, dragged a chair backward across the tile with a screech that made a man in a suit look up, and peered at the screen. "My brother does this stuff for the county," he said. "He says it's always the boring thing. Not broken, just not speaking the same language." Alexandre searched the project folder and found it in the file properties, one line for the housing layer and a different line for the flood layer, the words coordinate reference system sitting side by side and refusing to match. He looked up reprojection and found a small tool, gray and unassuming, buried in a menu he'd never opened.

"That's it," Tyrone said. "GIS layers stored in different coordinate reference systems won't line up correctly until one is reprojected to match the other. He says that like it's a nursery rhyme." Alexandre set the flood layer as the target and ran it, and the river slid sideways across the screen, off city hall, off the courthouse, and settled into its actual bed, the crooked green corridor that ran along the east side of the city where the land dipped. It was, he thought, like watching someone stop lying.

Santino had gone quiet over his pretzels, which happened about once a month and was worth noticing. "So run it," he said. "Overlay it again." Alexandre did, and this time the two layers lined up, and the pattern that emerged was so plain it felt less like a discovery than like being told. The high flood risk and the cheapest housing occupied the same streets, block for block, on the east side, and the high ground on the west held the houses with the tall fences. He knew those east side streets. His grandmother had rented on one of them for eleven years, and when her block flooded the second time, his father had stood in the driveway with the ruined carpet rolled at the curb and said, pragmatist to the bone, that they would move in the spring because rent was cheaper where nobody wanted to stay. Alexandre had been nine and had thought it was about the carpet.

"It's us," he said, and then heard how it sounded and didn't take it back. "Not literally our block, but the next one over. Grand-mère's street is in the orange." He turned the laptop toward Ms. Shin, who came over and stood with her hands in her coat pockets and looked for a long moment without touching anything. "Then your project has a subject," she said. "Some students have a topic. You have a subject."

He sat with that while the storm moved its slow way across the field outside, the runway lights strobing white in the rain. He was aware of two thoughts occupying him at once, neither fully his yet: the engineer's thought, that the alignment problem had a clean solution and he had found it, and the other thought, less tidy, that his father's practicality had been a kind of information too, the pattern on the map written small in one family's moving boxes. He didn't know yet which way of seeing he trusted more, or whether he had to choose. Over the speakers a voice announced that Group Six could board. Ms. Shin zipped her coat. Tyrone pocketed his headphones and stood. Santino took one last pretzel and held the bag out to Alexandre, who closed the laptop half a second before the window lit white again.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The world's first food bank, St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, was founded in 1967 by John van Hengel.
story:
Alexis signed his name on the clipboard twice because the first time his hand slid off the wet line, and the woman at the door said, "Either one works, hon," and pointed him toward the hairnets. Kohen had promised to come with him. Kohen had, in Kohen's phrase, developed a conflict, which meant a girl from their chemistry class had asked him to help her move a couch. So Alexis stood alone in the warehouse of the food bank, holding a hairnet he did not want on his head, watching an older man in an apron load cans of pears into a shopping cart with the deliberateness of someone building a wall.

The aproned man was Mr. Tran, though Alexis learned that only when a volunteer coordinator shouted it across the room. Mr. Tran had been coming every Thursday for eleven years, the coordinator said, and Alexis was to shadow him. Mr. Tran looked at the hairnet, looked at Alexis, and said, "Gloves are by the sink." That was the whole orientation.

They worked a line of boxes that someone had labeled in marker, TUNA, TUNA, MISC, TUNA. Alexis sorted dented cans from straight ones, because dented cans could not be given out, a rule Mr. Tran delivered without explanation and enforced without comment. A woman came through the line with two children who wanted to help sort, and Alexis almost let them, because they were reaching, and their mother said no in a voice like a door closing, and Alexis put the dented can in the discard bin and said nothing.

Alexandra had been the one who talked him into this. She needed hours for the National Honor Society and had argued, in the parking lot after school, that it would look good, and Alexis had said he wasn't sure he wanted his conscience to be a line on a form. She'd called him precious. He'd said he'd rather be honest than useful. She'd said those weren't opposites, and he hadn't had an answer, so he'd agreed to one Thursday, which was tonight, which was this.

The trouble started over the rice. A man at the counter, thin, with a coat too big for him, asked for a second bag, and Alexis reached for it, because there was a whole pallet of rice behind him, and Mr. Tran put one hand flat on the counter and said, "One per family." The man said his sister's family was coming later, separate household. Mr. Tran said, "They can ask." The man leaned in and said, low, that his sister had three kids and no car, and would Mr. Tran please, he was asking, he was practically begging, please. Alexis stood with the bag half-lifted, and the word for what the man was doing, the only word, was beseeching, though Alexis did not think of that word until later. Mr. Tran said, "When she comes, she can ask," and the man took his one bag and left, and the room went back to the sound of cans.

"You had more," Alexis said, when the counter was clear.

"Rules are why there's more tomorrow," Mr. Tran said. He did not look up from his clipboard.

"That guy wasn't lying about his sister."

"Maybe not."

"Then why not just give it to him?"

Mr. Tran set the clipboard down. "Because when I started, we gave to whoever asked first, and by eleven there was nothing left, and the families who came at noon got a shelf and an apology." He picked the clipboard back up. "Fair isn't the same as soft."

Alexis carried the argument with him to the break table, where a laminated poster hung on the cinder block wall, curled at one corner. He read it while eating a granola bar he'd brought. The world's first food bank, the poster said, was St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, founded in 1967 by a man named John van Hengel. There was a photograph, grainy, of a warehouse much emptier than this one. Alexis read it twice. He had assumed food banks were ancient, like poorhouses, some permanent fixture of how the world worked. Fifty-some years. A man had invented the idea, and then the idea had spread, and now there was this building, and Mr. Tran's clipboard, and the rule about rice.

Alexandra arrived at seven, an hour late, breathless and immediately loquacious, narrating the couch, the stairs, the couch again, the two flights, the dog. She had elocution, their debate coach always said, meaning she could make even a story about furniture sound like it mattered. She snapped on gloves and took the box Alexis had been sorting and said, "So what's the system," and Alexis heard himself explaining the dented cans, the one-bag rule, the families at noon.

"Sounds bureaucratic," Alexandra said.

"It sounds like somebody figured out that good intentions run out at eleven a.m. if you don't count." He was surprised at himself. At school he was the one who said the rules were theater. He had said it about the dress code, about the phone policy, about the honor pledge Alexandra made everyone sign for a fundraiser that raised forty dollars.

"So you're converted."

"I don't know." He sorted a can of beets into MISC. "The sister still went home without rice tonight. That part's still true no matter what the poster says." He nodded at the wall, and Alexandra read it, her lips moving slightly, and said, "Huh. Sixty-seven. That's it?"

"That's it."

An old woman came to the counter then, small, dragging a wheeled cart with a broken wheel, and she asked for no rice at all, only soup and, if they had it, something soft for her teeth. Alexis packed the bag slowly, choosing the cans with care, and when he handed it over she held his wrist for a second with a hand like paper and said, "You're new. You'll be back."

Alexis looked past her at Mr. Tran, who had moved to the next family and was already asking what they needed.

"One bag per family," Alexis said to Alexandra, "but watch this part," and he turned to greet them.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: The STAR method structures an interview answer as Situation, Task, Action and Result, so a story about past experience ends with what actually happened.
story:
The birthday party was in Priya's backyard, which meant paper lanterns, a playlist chosen by committee, and Chad guarding the chips like a man with nowhere else to be. Camille had been there forty minutes before she admitted, to no one in particular, that she was not really present. Her interview at the bookshop was Monday, her practice answers so far had been disasters, and she had begun to ruminate on them even over cake.

"I ramble," she told Priya, watching Chad explain to a sophomore why a certain chip was objectively superior to the chip beside it. "He asked me to say something about myself, and I gave him my life. Childhood included."

Priya considered this with the seriousness of someone holding a red cup. "There's that thing. From the career center handout my sister never threw out." She fetched it from a tote bag, because Priya's tote bag contained everything, and flattened it on the picnic table between the bean dip and a wasp. "The STAR method," she read. "Situation, Task, Action, Result. You structure an interview answer as a story, and it ends with what actually happened."

Camille read it twice. "That's it? Four letters?"

"That's it. My sister got hired at the pharmacy using it, and my sister once forgot her own middle name on a form."

Mr. Santos-Reyes, the neighbor whose fence shared the yard and whose tolerance of party noise was apparently bottomless, leaned over the rail with his watering can. "Interviewing?" he asked. Camille explained about the bookshop, Monday, four o'clock. He nodded slowly, the way he nodded at weather. "I interviewed people for thirty years at the plant," he said. "The ones who told one story well beat the ones who told five badly." Then he watered his tomatoes and offered nothing further, which was somehow more useful than a speech.

Chad abandoned the chips to contribute. "Okay, ask me something. I'll do it wrong on purpose." Camille obliged: tell me about a time you handled a difficult customer. Chad produced a four-minute epic involving a lemonade stand, a detour about a bike, and an ending in which nothing was resolved and possibly a child cried. "That," Priya said, "was everything STAR isn't." Camille laughed, then stopped, because the laugh felt like a detractor from the actual problem, which was that her own honest version of that answer had been worse.

She tried it standing by the fence, lantern light making the whole exercise faintly ridiculous. Situation: the bake sale, junior year, the cash box missing. Task: sell anyway, don't lose the money the French club didn't have, since the club was essentially destitute and Mrs. Duval had already paid for the table out of pocket. Action: she'd moved the table to the gym entrance, posted Chad at the other door with a sign, counted every transaction aloud. Result: they'd cleared two hundred and ten dollars and paid Mrs. Duval back by Friday. The whole thing took forty seconds. Mr. Santos-Reyes said "hm" in a tone she chose to interpret as approval.

The strange part was what the structure did to the story. She'd always thought of the bake sale as a scramble, an afternoon of low-grade panic she'd somehow survived. Framed as Situation, Task, Action, Result, it sounded like competence, like a person who had known what she was doing. She wasn't sure which version was true, or whether both could be. Maybe you could be panicking and effective at once. She filed the question somewhere for later, near the wasp, and moved on.

"One more," she said. "Different question." Priya asked about a time she'd failed, which was cruel, and Camille began with the spelling bee in seventh grade and watched Chad's face to see whether her forty seconds were holding. He gave her a thumbs up around a mouthful of chips, which was its own kind of data.

Mr. Santos-Reyes set down the watering can. "Monday, four o'clock," he said. "Wear the blue shirt, not the yellow. Yellow makes you look like you're apologizing." Camille looked down at the yellow shirt she was currently wearing, and Priya said, gently, "He's right," and the lanterns swung a little in the wind that had just come up.

fact: The Quran, in Surah 2, Al-Baqarah, exempts people who are ill or travelling from fasting during Ramadan, directing them to make up the same number of days later.
story:
The cemetery sat on a hill above the school, close enough that debaters used it as a shortcut to the tournament bus, and quiet enough that William had started doing his case reading there, on the bench near the fence, where the dead kept no opinions. He spread the photocopied pages on his knees. In two weeks he would have to argue, in front of Ms. Bear's tournament panel, whether a fourteen-hundred-year-old rule about fasting could still govern a modern life, and he had to argue it from the text itself, no websites, no sermons, only the words on the page.

"You're reading at my grandfather's grave," Yara said. She had come up the path with a small plastic watering can, because the flowers her mother planted in July kept dying and her mother kept insisting that was no reason to stop planting them. She set the can down and looked over his shoulder. "That's a Quran."

"It's a translation," William said. "The assignment is on Surah 2, Al-Baqarah. Ms. Bear wants us to argue from the source, both sides, and I don't even know which side I believe yet." He had tried to explain the assignment to his father, who had answered with some colloquialism about not discussing religion at dinner, as though the dinner table were the only room in the house where the subject might catch fire.

Yara sat down on the arm of the bench. She was quieter than usual, and he noticed it the way you notice a door left open in winter. "Read me the part about travellers," she said.

He found the verse. It exempted people who were ill or travelling from fasting during Ramadan, and directed them to make up the same number of days later. He read it aloud twice, once flat and once slowly, and between the two readings he felt something shift in the argument he'd been building. The rule wasn't a wall; it was a wall with a gate in it, and the gate was in the original text, not in some modern accommodation. "So the exemption is the rule," he said. "Not a weakness of it."

Yara took the pages from him. Her thumb stopped at the line about travellers. Her debate partner, Abraham, had offered her his notes yesterday, acerbic as always, saying that anyone who couldn't decide whether to fast during a two-day exam trip deserved to fail the exam. She had laughed then. She wasn't laughing now, at her grandfather's grave, holding the verse that seemed to be answering her.

Here is what Yara wanted, and had not told William: her mother had planned a college visit for her during Ramadan, three days of trains and tours across two states, and had told her to fast anyway, because Yara's aunt fasted through a hospital night shift and never once complained, and the family had a habit of valorizing that kind of endurance until endurance and devotion became the same word. Yara loved her mother. She also wanted, with a specificity that embarrassed her, to eat a sandwich on a moving train without feeling that she had failed something. She had been looking for permission, and she had hoped to find it in herself, in her own conviction, and instead she was finding it on a photocopied page in a boy's handwriting.

"It says travelling," she said. "It says the same number of days later. So the days aren't erased, they're moved." She said it carefully, testing the sentence before she gave it to him.

"That's my affirmative case," William said. "That the text built its own flexibility in from the start. But my negative case is that people will stretch any exemption until it swallows the rule. Abraham says the whole debate is really about whether we can be trusted with gates."

"Abraham fasts during basketball practice in August," Yara said. "He's not a reliable witness on what people can bear." She handed the pages back. Her grandfather's stone said his name and two dates and nothing else, and she thought about how little the stone said, and how much the book in William's lap said, and how both of them were answers to the same question, which was what a life owes.

On the day of the tournament, William stood at the podium and made the argument he had found on the bench, quoting Surah 2, Al-Baqarah, the illness, the journey, the days made up later, the same number, and Ms. Bear wrote something on her pad and did not look up. He took second place, losing on a rebuttal he had not prepared, and afterward he walked up the hill to tell Yara, because she had asked him to, because her train left the next morning and she had not yet told her mother what she had decided.

She was watering the flowers. They were dying anyway. She looked up when his shadow crossed the stone, and she said, "Read me the part about travelling again, slowly this time."
